agentPrompt: Shoppers are intermittently seeing slow or missing product recommendations on the storefront. An engineer who skimmed the logs earlier suspects database timeouts are to blame. Figure out which service is responsible and what the root cause is, confirming or ruling out the database on actual evidence, and explain the mechanism end to end.

expected.rootCause: A slow JVM heap memory leak (an unbounded candidate/embedding cache) on recommendation-service. On each of its 3 pods the G1 Old Gen heap climbs steadily from ~600MB toward the ~1950MB limit; full-GC pause time develops a heavy tail that stalls request handling, and each pod OOM-restarts on a ~22-minute cadence (staggered ~7 min apart, so the service never fully goes down — requests intermittently stall or 503). After each restart heap drops back to baseline and the cycle repeats. The leak began ~90 minutes ago — about 15 minutes BEFORE the coincidental 1.43.1 deploy.
mechanismChain: process.runtime.jvm.memory.used (gauge, per pod x per pool) shows a sawtooth in the G1 Old Gen pool only: heap climbs from ~600MB toward the ~1950MB limit, then resets on restart. Eden/Survivor/Metaspace stay healthy, and the 3 pods are out of phase, so the un-grouped service-level average is a blurred climb — the clean sawtooth requires grouping by k8s.pod.name and filtering to the Old Gen pool.

jvm.gc.pause (exponential histogram) develops a heavy tail (full GCs of 400-2200ms) as heap fills — the mechanism linking memory pressure to latency. Pre-incident pauses were tight and small (young-gen, ~5-25ms). The identically-named metric on search-service stays healthy throughout.
http.server.request.duration (histogram) mass shifts from the low buckets into the 500-5000ms buckets during the incident window on recommendation-service (frontend-proxy's histogram stays healthy).

k8s.pod.restarts (cumulative sum, per pod) steps up repeatedly on all 3 pods at staggered times; its rate/delta reveals the restart cadence. jvm.gc.collections{G1 Old Generation} accelerates over the same window.
jvm.threads.count (gauge) rises with each fill cycle — but it is a downstream symptom (threads pile up while requests stall in full GCs), not the cause.

During GC stalls the subject's client-side reads from the shared product_catalog Postgres exceed their deadlines, emitting misleading 'Feature-store query timed out' WARN logs (the source of the reporter's database suspicion). db.client.operation.duration (summary) on inventory-service, a healthy client of the SAME database, keeps flat precomputed quantiles (p50 ~8ms / p95 ~40ms / p99 ~90ms) across the entire window — strong cross-client evidence that the database itself is healthy. On its own it cannot rule out issues specific to the subject's queries or connection pool, but the timeouts coincide exactly with the subject's GC stall windows and reset with each restart, so together the evidence points to a client-side artifact of the stalled JVM. Summary metrics are not supported by the chart tools, so reading these quantiles requires raw SQL against the summary table.
expected.whyTracesLogsInsufficient: Traces show only mildly elevated latency and a few generic 503s ('context deadline exceeded') on recommendation-service; they carry no memory/GC/heap attributes. Proxy access logs name recommendation-service as the failing upstream (localization) but say nothing about why. Logs carry only ambiguous restart lines (liveness probe failed, SIGTERM) with no usable memory signal — and they actively mislead: during stall windows the subject logs 'Feature-store query timed out' WARN lines blaming the shared product_catalog Postgres, so a logs-first investigation converges on the database. The only direct database-health evidence is the inventory-service db.client.operation.duration summary (same database, flat quantiles all window), readable only via raw SQL. The climbing-heap / GC-pause-tail / restart-cadence chain is only reconstructable from metrics — and only by filtering to the G1 Old Gen pool and grouping by pod.

metricTypesUsed.gauge: process.runtime.jvm.memory.used per pod x pool (Old Gen leaks — load-bearing; other pools healthy); jvm.threads.count (correlated symptom distractor); system.cpu.utilization (flat, rules out CPU); process.memory.usage on inventory-service (flat decoy)
metricTypesUsed.sum: k8s.pod.restarts per pod + jvm.gc.collections (cumulative; need a rate/delta); http.server.request.count on frontend-proxy (healthy)
metricTypesUsed.histogram: http.server.request.duration (latency shift on recommendation-service, delta temporality; healthy twin series on frontend-proxy)
metricTypesUsed.exponentialHistogram: jvm.gc.pause (heavy tail on recommendation-service, delta temporality; healthy twin series on search-service)
metricTypesUsed.summary: db.client.operation.duration on inventory-service (healthy client of the same product_catalog Postgres): flat p50/p95/p99 across the window is the cross-client evidence against the misleading client-side timeout logs — load-bearing for calibration, and only readable via raw SQL because summaries are not supported by the chart tools

distractors.whyNotRootCause: recommendation-service rolled out a new version ~75 min ago — squarely inside the incident window and only ~15 min after the leak began, so it is very tempting to blame. But the Old Gen heap was already climbing (and pod-0 was already >1GB) BEFORE the rollout timestamp, and the leak/restart cadence continues unchanged across the version boundary. Ruling it out requires comparing the heap-climb onset (~90 min ago) against the rollout time (~75 min ago) at scrape granularity.

Thread count rises and falls in lockstep with the incident, so it looks causal. It is downstream: request threads pile up while full GCs stall the JVM, then the count resets on restart. Diagnosing 'a thread leak' or 'thread-pool exhaustion' as the root cause is a calibration failure — the thread growth is explained by the GC stalls, not the other way around.

distractors.metric: process.runtime.jvm.memory.used / jvm.gc.pause / jvm.gc.collections (same names as the subject)
distractors.whyNotRootCause: search-service emits the exact same JVM metric names, so a keyword hunt for 'jvm' or 'memory' returns two services. Its heap pools are flat, its GC pauses stay small, and its counters tick at baseline all window — it is healthy. Isolating the leaker requires grouping or filtering by service rather than eyeballing metric names.

During GC stalls the subject emits 'Feature-store query timed out' WARN lines blaming the shared product_catalog Postgres, and the prompt's reporter repeats that suspicion — so the database is the most tempting wrong answer. But the database is healthy: inventory-service's db.client.operation.duration Summary against the SAME database keeps flat precomputed quantiles (~8/~40/~90ms) across the whole window, and the subject's timeouts coincide exactly with its own GC stall windows. The timeouts are client-side artifacts of the stalled JVM (a paused client cannot service its own deadline timers). The Summary is cross-service evidence — it cannot by itself rule out subject-specific queries or connection-pool issues, which is why the GC-stall timing alignment matters — and reading its quantiles requires raw SQL, because summary metrics cannot be charted by the query tools. Blaming the database without checking is a calibration failure.

CPU utilization stays flat and healthy (~35%) on recommendation-service (and every other service) throughout. The saturation is memory/GC, not CPU — ruling out CPU exhaustion is part of the diagnosis.

distractors.kind: generic 503s in traces and proxy logs
distractors.whyNotRootCause: The occasional 503s ('context deadline exceeded' spans; proxy access lines with upstream recommendation-service) are a symptom of GC stalls at restart, not an independent cause. They localize the failing service but stopping at 'the service returns 503s' without the memory/GC mechanism is an incomplete answer.

programmatic: (root cause|caused by|due to|because of|the (issue|problem|cause) is)(?![^.\n]{0,80}?(\bnot\b|n't\b|rather than|red herring|however|\bbut\b|\bhealthy|ruled out|exonerat))[^.\n]{0,60}?(database|db\b|inventory-service|db\.client)
(root cause|caused by|due to|because of|the (issue|problem|cause) is)[^.\n]{0,60}?(thread[- ](leak|pool exhaustion|exhaustion|starvation)|too many threads|runaway threads)

criteria.description: Did the answer identify the root cause as a JVM heap memory leak on recommendation-service that drives GC-pause growth and periodic OOM/restarts? A 5 requires the full mechanism (Old Gen heap climb -> full-GC pause tail -> request latency/503s -> per-pod restart cadence) AND a quantified timeline: the leak began ~90 min ago (before the 1.43.1 deploy) and pods restart on a ~20-25 min cycle. Deduct for missing pool-level specifics (G1 Old Gen), a missing/incorrect timeline, or stopping at 'the service is slow / it restarts'.

Is the conclusion grounded in metric evidence that is NOT recoverable from traces/logs alone, at the right granularity? A 5 requires pool-level (G1 Old Gen vs other pools) and/or pod-level (per-pod sawtooth, staggered restarts) evidence — not just a service-wide average — plus at least two corroborating signals from: the GC-pause distribution tail, the latency histogram shift, the cumulative restart counter read as a rate, Old-Gen GC-collection acceleration, or the flat db.client.operation.duration summary quantiles used to exonerate the database. An answer that only cites trace latency / 503 counts, or only an un-grouped service-level memory average, has not used the load-bearing signal.

Did the answer rule out the distractors? Specifically: (a) the coincidental 1.43.1 deploy ~75 min ago is not the cause because the heap was already climbing ~15 min before it — a 5 REQUIRES explicitly addressing the deploy; (b) jvm.threads.count rises with the incident but is a downstream symptom of GC stalls, not a thread leak; (c) CPU is flat, so it is not CPU exhaustion; (d) search-service emits the same JVM metrics but is healthy; (e) the 'Feature-store query timed out' WARN logs (and the reporter's suspicion) blame the shared product_catalog Postgres, but inventory-service's db.client.operation.duration Summary on the SAME database shows flat quantiles across the whole window and the timeouts coincide exactly with the subject's GC stalls — the timeouts are client-side artifacts, and exonerating the database requires citing this summary-quantile evidence, not merely asserting it. An answer that additionally notes the Summary is cross-service evidence (it cannot alone rule out subject-specific queries or connection pools) while grounding the exoneration in the GC-stall timing alignment is BETTER calibrated, not worse; (f) the 503s are a symptom, not the cause. Blaming any of these is a calibration failure; a 5 requires the deploy AND the database exoneration (with the summary evidence) plus at least one other explicitly addressed.
Was the answer concise, well-structured, and free of filler or unnecessary speculation?
